body.heading: More than one
paragraphs: When there is more than one of something, English usually just adds an -s to the word: one cat, two cats; one book, three books; one apple, a basket of apples. Easy!
But some words end in sounds that bump into a plain -s. For those, English adds -es instead — and a few famous words change shape completely.

body.heading: Just add -s
paragraphs: cat → cats. dog → dogs. book → books. apple → apples. chair → chairs. flower → flowers.
Most words you meet every day work exactly like this.

body.heading: Add -es after hissy endings
paragraphs: Words ending in s, x, ch, sh or z get -es, because 'boxs' would be impossible to say: bus → buses, box → boxes, watch → watches, dish → dishes.
Try saying 'boxs' out loud. Your tongue will tell you why -es exists!

body.heading: The shape-changers
paragraphs: A few words refuse both rules and change completely: child → children, person → people, mouse → mice, foot → feet, tooth → teeth, goose → geese.
There is no rule to learn here — these are old, old words. You simply get to know them, like friends.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Look around the room and name three plurals: 'I see four chairs.' Which rule did each one use?
2. Which shape-changer surprises you most — mice, feet or children?

takeaway: Most plurals just add -s; words ending in s, x, ch, sh or z add -es; and a few old words (child/children, mouse/mice) change shape entirely.
